“Rogue waves” over 25 meters tall can appear suddenly, even in calm seas.
“Giant’s Causeway” in Northern Ireland formed from cooling lava into over 40,000 hexagonal basalt columns.
The “Singing Beach” in Massachusetts literally squeaks when you walk on dry sand.
“Waterspouts” are tornadoes that form over bodies of water, connecting sea and sky in spinning columns.
“Rainbow fogbows” are white or faintly colored bows appearing in fog instead of rain.
“Ghost rain” or “virga” is precipitation that evaporates before hitting the ground.
“Black rain” fell after Hiroshima’s bombing, a toxic mix of soot and water vapor.
Earthquake booms, low rumbling sounds, sometimes occur before seismic shifts.
“Stone forests” in Madagascar’s Tsingy de Bemaraha are razor-sharp limestone pinnacles shaped by erosion.
“Pillar lightning” can connect multiple clouds in a single vertical shaft.
“Green snow algae” can alter polar melting by darkening the surface and absorbing more heat.
“Desert glass” found in Egypt formed from ancient meteor impacts melting sand.
“Watermelon snow” appears pink and smells sweet, thanks to pigmented algae in melting snowfields.
Moonbows, rainbows created by moonlight, are rare, faint arcs visible on bright full-moon nights.
“Horsetail Falls” in California glows orange each February when sunset light mimics fire on its cascade.
“Basalt columns” appear worldwide, like Devil’s Postpile or Fingal’s Cave, a geometric proof of volcanic cooling symmetry.
“Colorful geothermal terraces” in Yellowstone’s Grand Prismatic Spring form from microbial mats living in extreme heat.
The “Lightning Volcano” Sakurajima in Japan erupts with plasma storms during explosions.
“Petrifying wells” in England turn objects to stone by mineral deposits from flowing water.
“Underwater rivers” flow beneath the ocean in dense saline layers, complete with banks and currents.
“Black smokers” on the ocean floor spew superheated water and minerals, sustaining unique life forms.
“Sulfuric acid rain” occasionally falls near active volcanoes, corroding surfaces instantly.
“Ice tsunamis” occur when frozen lake ice piles onto shore in huge walls.
“Fire rainbows” aren’t rainbows at all, they’re circumhorizontal arcs seen only at high latitudes.
The “Magnetic anomaly” of Bangui (Central Africa) is one of Earth’s most intense, possibly from an ancient meteor impact.
Earth’s hum, a continuous low-frequency vibration, resonates globally even when no earthquakes occur.
